first_remarks.remarks_to_the_author:
In this manuscript, the authors present an experimental and simulation study, where they investigate the effect of differences in cell length on the segregation of and competition between two bacterial strains, using E. coli mutants as a model system, as they grow over an agar plate. The main claims of the authors are that:

(1) The longer WT cells win the competition while spreading via growth on the agar, which is well supported by the results. (2) This advantage of longer cells comes from the nematic alignment of the longer cells with each other which allows a rapid directional spreading towards the edge of the colony, where fresh nutrients are available that allow them to outgrow the shorter cells at the edge and take over the propagation front. Here, major concerns can be raised. Indeed, although this mechanism is in principle plausible, over several previous rounds of revisions in which I participated, the relative consensus between the reviewers was that the evidence was not solid enough to rule out alternative mechanisms.

In particular, there appears to be more elongated than short cells at the edge of the colony from the start, which the reviewers interpreted as a possible coffee-ring-like effect that would enrich longer cells from the start. I did not find the authors' response on the coffee-ring effect fully satisfactory: If the balance of physical parameters that allows coffee-ring suppression and exclusion from the edge for long colloids in the PS system of Yunker et al was the same in bacteria, one would expect no coffee ring for rod-shaped bacteria. This is not the case, even when the cells are non-motile, as evidenced by many papers including the ones cited by the authors.

In the previous rounds of revision, I suggested to follow the cell ratio over time at the edge of the colony from the time of inoculation onward. The authors provided Fig. S10, which shows a gradual takeover of the longer cells over time and strengthens the case of the authors. However the record is shown only 11h after the initial spot inoculation. This hides the early dynamics, and prevents us from understanding whether an initial coffee ring effect is present. Moreover, it was done for a very small fraction of longer cells. I would like to see the early dynamics and the initial ratio of longer cells at the edge, also for higher fraction of longer cells. This would resolve whether a coffee-ring effect can be considered as an alternative explanation.

Regarding the concerns raised by the other referee about the possibility of nematic ordering and then its role in the takeover, be it the main driver or an action in synergy with a coffee-ring effect, I think the best way to resolve the matter is experimentally. Figure 2D suggests that long cells align towards the edge in the middle of the colony and along the edge at the front, which would support a role of nematic alignment for gaining the front faster and then to block the other cells there. Unfortunately, this is only one time point and a single condition, as well as apparently the characterization of a single replicate. I thus suggest to carry a full and exhaustive characterization of the distribution of orientations at these different positions across the colony, for all conditions (WT/AK, WT/AS, and AK/AS), several time points as the colony develops, and averaged over several replicates. This would undoubtedly greatly help confirm (or infirm) the authors' proposed mechanism.

I also note that the distribution of theta runs from -80 to 80 for the simulations (Fig2B), but from -100 to 100 for the experiments (Fig 2D). What is the unit of theta? And if it is degrees, why does it not run from -90 to +90 as one would expect?

Other minor points:

The legend of Movie 4 still does not indicate the initial ratio, which should be zeta=1 from the previous round of revision

On the Malthusian ratio, I still find the new wording ('fold-change' alone) slightly confusing, I would recommend using 'foldchange in total OD' for better clarity

In discussion, about the sentence 'However, our results suggest that in other natural habitats such as on surfaces, in soils, and animal tissue, … the advantageous morphology is the rod shape'. In soil and tissue, the upper surface of the colony is often not exposed to air, as is the case on surfaces and in the experiments here, but rather to a potentially nutritious milieu. The data of Smith et al. suggest that in these cases nutrient supply from the top might change the behavior radically. Please nuance.

In sum, if the authors can revise their manuscript appropriately and address the raised major points thoroughly, they would have in my opinion a good case for publication in Nature communications.

(Remarks on code availability)

4. Considering the response of the authors to both referees' comments, I think there are a few points that need further clarification before the paper can be considered for publication:
5. 1 I find that the WT overtake by nematic alignment is still relatively poorly characterized in experiments. The distributions of orientation in Fig 2D correspond to only one time point and a single condition, as well as apparently a single replicate. I suggest to carry an exhaustive characterization of the distribution of orientations theta at the different distances from the colony front, for all conditions (WT/AK, WT/AS, and AK/AS), several time points as the colony develops, and averaged over several replicates. The authors have shown that they have the raw data, so the image analysis should be feasible in a reasonable time. This would undoubtedly greatly strengthen (or infirm) the authors' proposed mechanism.

I also note that the distribution of theta runs from -80 to 80 for the simulations (Fig2B), but from -100 to 100 for the experiments (Fig 2D). What is the unit of theta? And if it is degrees, why does it not run from -90 to +90 as one would expect?

- 2 On the model, my feeling is that the authors again did not directly and fully answer the other referee's question. They now proposed very assertively a more precise picture of the alignment mechanism, but without backing it with additional simulations or data that would be needed. I think they should be either more careful with formulation of what are at this point hypotheses, or show data that demonstrate their claims. This concerns:

- The mechanism of nematic alignment of long cells to the long/short domain boundaries is not demonstrated in this system. Is there an increased ordering/nematicity next to boundaries compared to within the domain in the experiments and/or simulations? ## Reviewer #2

The authors have revised their manuscript according to our comments. Since we have already gone through multiple rounds of revision, I will only focus on the last points.

I however regret that it only starts 11 h after inoculation, which hides the early dynamics and the initial ratio. The dynamics at several initial inoculation ratios would also have been nice.

Instead, a front that was fully dominated by shorter bacteria gets populated by the longer cells. Remarkably, we find that the ensemble average of strength, S(t), evolves linearly. 2.     Regarding radial alignment of the nematic arms: The authors seem to have misunderstood the model and conclusions of Dell'Arciprete et al. (2018). While the equations they provide recapitulate the model in 1D and in 2D, the crucial point they omit in the 2D case is that the sign of  in the key equation (in the third-to-last line of the new section in the SI, page 8; Dell'Arciprete et al. denote this by ) plays a critical role in determining the steady-state. If the growth-induced flow is compressible, then and there is a stable steady-state at . However, what Dell'Arciprete et al. found in their data is that the flow is incompressible, , and there is no radial alignment. Instead, Dell'Arciprete et al. found that their bacterial colonies feature only nematically ordered 'microdomains' whose length scale roughly corresponds to the cell length. As I described in my last review, the conditions that give rise to radial alignment are not trivial: they critically depend on the nature of the growth-induced flow. For instance, Nijjer et al. (doi: 10.1038/s41467-021-26869-6) showed that verticalization in the core of growing biofilmswhich affects the in-plane growth-induced flow experienced by cells in the basal layer by introducing a 'growth void' in the core-causes radial alignment in the periphery; without this perturbation to the growth-induced flow, radial alignment does not occur. As such, the explanations that the authors provide here are incorrect.

We would like to thank the referee for pointing this out. The referee is correct in that previous work clearly shows that uniform growth of single-species bacteria cannot induce a strain-rate or vorticity tensor, which induces long-range nematic order (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-26869-6). With this realization, we looked at our single-species data. Upon closer inspection of supplementary Figure 13, where we investigated WT-WT mixtures, we indeed observed that no radial ordering seems to emerge. Similarly, in particle simulations, which now have been added as supplementary Fig. S14 (see below) of single-specie elongated bacteria, we again see no obvious radial alignment.

Fig. S14 Representative snapshots of a mono-strain simulation with longer bacteria (aspect ratio l/w =4) after 7.1 generations. We remark that there is less nematic alignment than in the simulations with l\_L/l\_S =4 (Fig 2A) , only small patches of local nematic order where observed with no global radial symmetry.

![Image](s41467-025-67791-5_artifacts\image_000004_0c78c1c4a4d869b62a990b6a93ec10088ae7fab46f9a3d38e497e08be4ad5dfc.png)

Nijjer et al. did show that it is possible to induce radial nematic order by breaking the radial uniform growth by for example introducing a growth void in the core . In our case, the radial alignment comes from the isotropic/nematic interaction between the two species, with the isotropic domain playing the role of void.

Previous work has shown that the interface between isotropic and active nematic mixtures can induce strain tensors, which makes the director of the nematic align with the interface

(https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2106038118) due to local density symmetry breaking (similar to local growth voids), which induces an effective active anchoring

(https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.113.248303). Because the interface between two expanding species is radial, this additional strain-rate tensor from the isotropic-nematic interface causes the nematic to align radially and leads to similar effects of bacteria slinging in confined channels (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.0050302).

We have now addressed this properly in the manuscript by including the above in the section Alignment-induced mechanism gives longer… :

'Due to uni-axial growth, active forces cause elongated bacteria to align along interfaces with the shorter bacteria (19) and form radially aligned patches in the direction of growth (detailed in Supplementary Information). These interface boundaries orientationally guide the bacteria into channels (20),which connect the homeland to the outer rim of the colony and form a channel for longer bacteria to reach the front. '

Furthermore, as explained in the reply to the minor comment below we have further used our continuum model to clarify and support this point. Therefore we rewrote the final paragraph of Takeover rate is set by differences…:

'Specifically, nematic bacteria align at the boundaries formed with isotropic bacteria and this alignment is diminished, when neighbouring bacteria are weakly nematic themselves. For Instance, the radial expansion of isotropic AK patches directs the chain-formation of WT into the nematic arms (Fig.S8).The takeover rate is independent of the length of the individual bacteria, but only when the orientational packing of the monoculture is the same (i.e.,both species are within the nematic phases). When, due to their individual lengths, the shortest bacteria species transition from isotropically packed to nematically ordered state, the takeover rate drops. This radial alignment effect disappears in single species colonies (Supplementary Fig.S13 andFig. S14.), as the incompressible radial expansion flow,in the absence of interspecies interfaces, does not induce radial alignment (18,34).'

## Minor:

3. Regarding the continuum model: While I understand the authors' point that removing injection of biomass due to growth from the continuum model is useful for 'highlight[ing] a distinct collective mechanical mechanism' (lines 118-119 in the new manuscript), I believe the model-based analysis is incomplete without a model that actually tries to explain the data. If cells are growing at the front (which they clearly are), then such growth should be included in at least one version of the model. Moreover, the authors suggest that the model was formulated without growth to illustrate that the proposed takeover mechanism is independent of 'any possible number advantage in inoculation,' but imposing equal growth rates to the two species would not necessarily introduce a number advantage to either, and should not be conflated with the issue with a number advantage at the front due to, e.g., the coffee-ring effect. The authors' illustration of a growth-independent mechanical mechanism is interesting, but I believe that, without consideration of a version of the model with growth, this analysis is incomplete.

To address the point of using the continuum model to explain the data, we actually performed continuum simulations mimicking a single species to contrast with the two-species continuum model to highlight that the isotropic-nematic interfaces are indeed the cause of the radial alignment.

Similar to  Nijjer et al. (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-26869-6), we find no nematic preference in the radial direction for the single species simulations in Fig. A (see below). This is in contrast to the variation of nematic alignment properties (mimicking the difference in aspect ratio of the two species) in the continuum simulations, which is enough to induce alignment along the interfaces even without an effective growth term.

This result is similar to the two-phase model of Nijjer et al., but rather than transforming an in-plane aligned species into a vertical alignment species (causing an isotropic core), we use the continuum model to show that the introduction of different nematic strengths between species is already enough to induce radial alignment. This is important as we do not observe verticalization of our experimental bacteria, so that cannot be the term that causes the radial alignment.

Fig. A: Probability density function (PDF) of the nematic radial orientation for two species (blue).

While we believe that this reveals the primary mechanism for inducing radial expansion when two strains compete, we note that the alignment in the continuum model is rather weak, as the interfaces are only weakly radially outwards. The inclusion of the growth term would drive the interfaces to more strongly expand outwards in the radial direction.

We thank the reviewer for giving us the possibility to strengthen the relation between nematic ordering and radial alignment. In the present version of our manuscript, we have re-analyzed our data and added new to emphasize the connection and strengthen our proposed mechanism.

In the original manuscript, we showed how the nematic alignment of the wild-type (WT) and the shortest mutant (AK) changes within the first hours of colony-formation (Fig. 2E and S10B), going from similar distributions of the order parameter to high local alignment of WT - considerably less for AK, in accordance with prior studies [doi:10.1103/PhysRevX.8.031065]. - 2 On the model, my feeling is that the authors again did not directly and fully answer the other referee's question. They now proposed very assertively a more precise picture of the alignment mechanism, but without backing it with additional simulations or data that would be needed. I think they should be either more careful with formulation of what are at this point hypotheses, or show data that demonstrate their claims. This concerns:
- The role of biomass increase, which they argue without showing would be too slow to explain the alignment. Including simulations of the continuous model that include it, as previously suggested, would be a great way to show this. Also, why would the bacteria orient first radially and then perpendicularly to the edge, if biomass increase and thus colony expansion do not play a role, as the authors seem to argue?

As suggested by the referee, we address this point by more carefully articulating the hypotheses in the revised manuscript, because extending the continuum model to include biomass increase would require significant modification of the model to extend it from binary fields to at least three-phase fields, allowing for an expanding interface.

We now clearly describe the key mechanisms that lead to the longer bacteria eventually overtaking the smaller ones at the front.

- Biomass expansion leads to the formation of radial interfaces between the smaller and larger bacteria.
- The larger bacteria align at any interface (either with the agar surrounding or the shorter, less nematically aligned bacteria), through a process called active anchoring,. (https://doi.org/10.1039/C7SM00325K, https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.102.020601, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2106038118, https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.74.030904). This arises from gradients in nematic ordering at interfaces where the active agents generate forces, either through self-motility or cell division.
- Due to this alignment, larger bacteria tend to deposit more at the colony front through the channels formed along these radial interfaces. This is why  in both the particle simulation and experiments we see small regions of longer bacteria starting to form regions at the colony front .

These bumps eventually subside as the longer bacteria reorient themselves at the interface, allowing them to overtake the entire front of the colony (Similar behaviour in bacteria where species have different division rates https://doi.org/10.1038/s41559-018-0734-9 and https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1809587115).

We emphasize that the purpose of the continuum model is to demonstrate how the longer bacteria, through an active anchoring mechanism, can compete at the interface. The model does not capture the initial radial expansion and, as a result, does not produce radial sector boundaries. Instead, the increased activity of the active material enables mixing between species. The phase corresponding to the longer bacteria can advect toward the front, where they align with the interface. This alignment allows them to once again dominate the outer region.

This advective, active mixing mechanism bypasses the need for biomass deposition, which is why the longer bacteria overtake the front in both experiments and particle-based simulations. Recent work on active mixing in particle-based models driven by reduced friction shows behavior consistent with our continuum model, in which no radial interfaces are observed ( https://doi.org/10.1101/2025.01.22.634274)

However, we stress that neither the experiments nor the particle-based model presented here exhibit such active mixing. This is evident from the persistence of radial sector boundaries, which are typically disrupted under strong active mixing ( https://doi.org/10.1101/2025.01.22.634274).

As suggested by the referee, we have clarified this point in the revised manuscript, discussing the limitations of the biphasic continuum model, and which specific predictions this model makes, and differences with our particle model, which allows for biomass increase.

- The mechanism of nematic alignment of long cells to the long/short domain boundaries is not demonstrated in this system. Is there an increased ordering/nematicity next to boundaries compared to within the domain in the experiments and/or simulations? Does the ordering propagate from the edges to the center of long cell cluster?

Indeed, as the referee correctly points out, in addition to the interface at the front of the colony, a secondary interface forms between the long and short bacterial domains within the bulk. At this internal interface, the active anchoring mechanism aligns the longer bacteria along the boundary. As shown in the manuscript (Fig. 3D), this alignment enables the longer bacteria to overtake the shorter ones, particularly when the latter exhibit weaker nematic order.

We emphasize that active anchoring is a well-established mechanism (https://doi.org/10.1039/C7SM00325K, https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.102.020601, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2106038118, https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.74.030904) and it can be understood by decomposing the active forces into components parallel and perpendicular to the interface with normal m and tangent vector t between nematic and isotropic regions with gradients of the nematic order and nematic orientation n. |∇𝑞|
